scenes.headline: How SAM 3.1 tracks sixteen objects in one pass
scenes.sub: Object Multiplex, Meta's shared-memory rewrite of the SAM 3 video tracker.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Mocha! SAM 3 tracks every object in a video, and its cost grew with each one it tracked. Here's how SAM 3.1 shares the work.

scenes.text: SAM 3 ran a memory path for every tracked object. Object Multiplex packs up to sixteen objects into a bucket, and runs it once per bucket.
scenes.say: SAM 3 ran a memory path for every tracked object. Object Multiplex packs up to sixteen objects into a bucket, and runs it once per bucket.

steps.say: The frame is encoded once, as before. Then up to sixteen objects' masks are packed into one bucket, and encoded together into one shared spatial memory.
What keeps the objects apart is a small embedding for each one, stored in the memory bank beside the shared features.
Memory attention and the mask decoder run once for the whole bucket. Each object's embedding is simply added to its mask queries.

steps.note: objects in a frame mostly occupy different places
steps.say: Demux hands every object its own mask. Sharing works because sixteen objects in a frame mostly sit in sixteen different places.

scenes.title: Why the number is a slope
scenes.say: Fit a straight line to Meta's own eight measured points, and frame time looks like this.

parts.note: the fixed floor: the backbone, shared all along
parts.say: Twenty-nine milliseconds is the floor: the backbone, which both versions always shared.
Each extra object adds under half a millisecond. SAM 3 paid four point six four five.

scenes.title: Speedup over an optimized SAM 3
scenes.say: So the speedup depends on where you stand. At one object it's about seven percent slower. At a hundred and twenty-eight, five point two times faster.

scenes.text: The speedup is a slope, not a constant: the same backbone floor, with a far cheaper cost per extra object.

recap: Sixteen objects share one memory pass
The gain grows with the object count
scenes.say: To recap: sixteen objects share one memory pass, small embeddings keep them apart, and the gain grows with every object.
